analysis.one_liner: Mandates 100% clean electricity, zero-emission vehicles, and electrified trains by 2035 and ends fossil fuel subsidies and exports.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote in any of the seven committees it was sent to, and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would force a rapid shift off fossil fuels: 80% of electricity, new cars, and rail from clean sources by 2027, and 100% by 2035. It would block new federal permits for major fossil fuel projects starting in 2018, repeal tax breaks for oil and gas drilling, ban exports of US crude oil and natural gas, and make wind and solar tax credits permanent. It pairs those mandates with aid for the people on the losing side: permanent funding to weatherize low-income homes, up to three years of wage, health, and pension support for displaced fossil fuel workers, and billions of dollars for economic development in coal country.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near polluting facilities, low-income households that would get weatherization and efficiency retrofits, coal and other fossil fuel workers who would receive wage, health, pension, and retraining support during a transition, and communities in coal country that would receive infrastructure and reclamation funds. The wind and solar industries would gain permanent tax credits and guaranteed demand from the mandates.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income households, fossil fuel workers, polluted communities

how_it_helps.text: Requires 80% of electricity, new vehicle sales, and rail lines/engines to come from clean or zero-emission sources by 2027, and 100% by 2035.

Prohibits new federal permits for major fossil fuel projects — power plants, pipelines, refineries, terminals, and exploration — beginning in 2018, and voids permits granted after February 2017 that used eminent domain or skipped tribal consultation.
Repeals oil and gas tax breaks, including expensing of intangible drilling costs, percentage depletion, and the domestic production deduction.
Permanently extends and makes refundable the wind production tax credit and the solar investment tax credit, with no phaseout.
Bans exports of domestically produced crude oil and natural gas, including LNG.
Permanently funds the Weatherization Assistance Program at $1.5 billion per year to retrofit low-income homes, cutting their energy bills.

Provides displaced fossil fuel workers up to three years of unemployment insurance, health care, and pension support tied to their prior salary, plus retraining and relocation assistance, and targets $40 million a year to Appalachian communities, $250 million a year to reclaim abandoned mine lands, and roughly $7 billion over 10 years for water, broadband, and grid infrastructure in coal counties.

Creates a Labor Department workforce center prioritizing jobs for displaced fossil fuel workers and residents of disadvantaged communities, and funds the programs by repealing offshore tax deferral for multinational corporations and redirecting the repealed fossil fuel tax credits.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal companies, which would lose tax subsidies, face a permit moratorium, and lose export markets; vehicle manufacturers and railroads, which would have to convert their fleets on a ten-year timeline; and possibly consumers, if rapid mandated electrification raises energy prices before clean technology fully scales.

drawbacks.text: The timeline is aggressive: the bill itself acknowledges that replacing baseload power with storage technologies that are 'mostly in their early stages' would require significant funding and breakthroughs to reach 100% clean electricity by 2035.

Banning crude and LNG exports and halting new fossil fuel permits immediately would cut off revenue and jobs in oil, gas, and coal regions years before the bill's worker-transition and coal-country programs are proven to replace them, and could raise fuel prices for consumers.

Requiring 80% of all new vehicle sales to be zero-emission by 2027 and full rail electrification by 2035 imposes conversion costs on manufacturers and railroads that could show up in vehicle and freight prices.

The bill's funding depends on repealing offshore corporate tax deferral and redirecting repealed fossil fuel tax breaks, which are one-time revenue changes funding permanent annual spending programs of well over $2 billion a year.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers real, targeted benefits to ordinary people — home retrofits that cut energy bills, guaranteed support for displaced workers, and cleanup money for coal country — while the main costs fall on fossil fuel companies, which it deliberately strips of subsidies and market access. The honest risk is pacing: mandating an 80% clean transition by 2027 is far faster than the technology and grid investments the bill itself says are needed, so households could face higher energy prices in the interim. Whether the tradeoff is worth it depends heavily on how quickly clean generation and storage could actually scale.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on September 1, 2017 and sent to seven different House committees, none of which ever held a hearing, marked it up, or sent it to the floor, and it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Tulsi Gabbard introduced the bill on September 1, 2017, with Reps. Raskin, Lee, Barragán, and Ted Lieu as original cosponsors.

The Speaker referred it to seven committees at once — Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, Education and the Workforce, Science, Space, and Technology, Financial Services, and Foreign Affairs — splitting its jurisdiction so broadly that no single committee owned it.
Within days, portions were referred to three Transportation subcommittees and, a week later, to the Energy and Commerce Energy Subcommittee; another Energy Subcommittee referral followed in May 2018.
The record shows no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action through the end of the 115th Congress in January 2019.
Support was entirely Democratic: 47 cosponsors joined Gabbard, and no Republican signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel companies kept their tax subsidies, permitting pipeline, and export markets, and automakers and railroads avoided conversion mandates; no one got the bill's clean energy mandates, weatherization funding, or worker protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and their allied industries

for.name: Rep. Tulsi Gabbard

sides.party_line_note: All 48 supporters — Gabbard and her 47 cosponsors — were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and no roll-call was ever taken because the bill never left committee.

industries.note: The bill repeals their core tax subsidies, halts federal permits for new pipelines, refineries, terminals, and drilling, and bans crude and LNG exports. Its legislative findings explicitly target the industry's tax loopholes and lobbying spending.

industries.industry: Solar and wind energy developers and manufacturers
industries.note: Permanent, refundable production and investment tax credits plus mandated 100% clean electricity give the industry guaranteed, growing demand. Every retail electric supplier becomes a customer by 2035.

Utilities selling over 1,000 MWh must hit 80% clean electricity by 2027 and 100% by 2035, a costly compliance burden for fossil-heavy suppliers. Suppliers able to buy or generate clean power gain a protected market; the bill funds grid modernization to help them get there.

Each manufacturer selling 100+ vehicles must make 80% of sales zero-emission by 2027 and 100% by 2035, forcing rapid, expensive fleet conversion. A new car allowance rebate system would subsidize consumers to buy those vehicles, so mandates create the market the industry must serve.
Rail lines and locomotives must be 80% electrified by 2027 and 100% by 2035, and diesel engines are banned from operating after 2035. The capital cost of full electrification falls on the railroads.

industries.industry: Low-income home retrofit and weatherization contractors
industries.note: Permanent $1.5 billion annual funding for the Weatherization Assistance Program creates a steady stream of federally funded retrofit work in low-income homes.
